title: Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Mother
paragraphs:
Your Children Hear the Way You Talk About Their Mother
Before your children ever ask you what love should look like, they have already been studying the way you look at her.
There is a lesson being taught in your house that may never appear in a family devotional.
No whiteboard.
No sermon.
No carefully prepared speech.
Just a father speaking to his wife.
And children listening.
They hear the joke you make at her expense.
They hear the irritation buried underneath your voice.
They notice the eye roll.
They notice when she starts explaining something and you interrupt before she can finish.
They notice whether you speak about her with tenderness when she leaves the room—or whether her absence becomes permission to dishonor her.
They hear the sarcastic comment you thought was harmless.
They see the expression on her face afterward.
And perhaps most frightening of all...
they are learning.
A little boy sitting at your table may be silently learning how a husband talks to a woman.
A little girl in the back seat may be silently learning what kind of treatment a woman is supposed to tolerate from a man who says he loves her.
You may think they are playing.
You may think they are watching television.
You may think they are too young to understand.
But children do not have to understand marriage theology to absorb the atmosphere of a marriage.
Long before you give them relationship advice...
they have been watching yours.
That is why the words of Paul to husbands should land with far more weight than sentimental Christianity sometimes gives them:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας...”
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas...
“Husbands, love your wives...”
But Paul does not stop there.
He gives husbands a terrifyingly beautiful standard:
“...καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“...just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
Read that again slowly.
Not merely:
Love your wife when she is agreeable.
Not:
Love her when she speaks your love language.
Not:
Love her when the house is peaceful, the finances are stable, intimacy is easy, and she appreciates everything you do.
Paul points the husband toward Christ.
That changes everything.
The Greek verb translated “love” is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate, from agapaō.
And notice what Paul does with that command.
He does not leave “love” floating in the air as an undefined romantic feeling.
He anchors it to Jesus Christ.
“Love your wives...
as Christ loved the church.”
Then Paul explains what that Christ-shaped love did.
Christ gave Himself for her.
That means biblical husbandhood cannot be reduced to earning money, occupying a position, demanding respect, winning arguments, or announcing that the Bible calls the husband the head of the wife.
The model standing before the Christian husband is a crucified Savior.
Jesus did not merely speak about love.
He gave Himself.
And somewhere in your home, your children are watching whether the Christianity you confess on Sunday survives the way you speak to their mother on Tuesday night.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because you can know Scripture and still weaponize sarcasm.
You can lead prayer and still humiliate your wife.
You can provide financially and still make her feel emotionally unsafe.
You can tell your sons to respect women while allowing them to watch you belittle the most important woman in their childhood.
You can tell your daughter never to settle for a man who disrespects her...
while teaching her, by example, that disrespect is simply something wives learn to endure.
Children notice contradictions adults learn to excuse.
They remember tone.
They remember tension.
They remember the strange silence after Dad said something cruel and everyone suddenly became interested in their food.
They remember Mom walking into another room.
They remember Dad laughing.
They remember wondering whether they were supposed to laugh too.
And sometimes a child begins carrying lessons nobody intentionally taught.
“Maybe this is marriage.”
“Maybe men speak this way when they are angry.”
“Maybe women are supposed to absorb humiliation.”
“Maybe love means staying while somebody continually tears you down.”
“Maybe saying sorry is weakness.”
“Maybe whoever speaks loudest wins.”
Then twenty years pass.
The child becomes an adult.
And Dad is confused by the relationship choices his son or daughter makes.
But sometimes the child is simply repeating a language first heard at home.
Father...
your children hear the way you talk about their mother.
And they hear the way you talk to her.
That does not mean your children need to witness a fake marriage.
They do not need parents pretending never to disagree.
Healthy marriage is not the absence of conflict.

Your children may actually learn something profoundly valuable from seeing two imperfect people disagree without contempt, tell the truth without cruelty, apologize without excuses, forgive without keeping score, and return to Christ when pride gets between them.
Imagine what happens when a son hears his father say:
“I was wrong.”
Imagine what happens when a daughter watches her father approach her mother after an argument and say:
“The way I spoke to you was sinful. Please forgive me.”
Do you understand what that child just witnessed?
Not weakness.
The Gospel.
Sin acknowledged.
Pride surrendered.
Grace requested.
Forgiveness practiced.
Relationship restored.
This is Christianity where children can see it.
And maybe that is where some fathers reading this need to stop pretending.
Maybe you have never hit your wife.
Maybe you have never abandoned your family.
Maybe you have remained financially responsible.
And because of that, you have quietly given yourself a passing grade.
But contempt can live inside respectable homes.
Mockery can sit at Christian dinner tables.
Cruelty does not always scream.
Sometimes it smirks.
Sometimes it sighs.
Sometimes it makes “jokes” everyone knows are not really jokes.
Sometimes it says:
“You always do this.”
“You never understand.”
“What is wrong with you?”
Sometimes it publicly tells an embarrassing story about her because everybody laughs.
Sometimes it compares her with another woman.
Sometimes it dismisses her concerns as dramatic.
Sometimes it corrects her in front of the children simply to establish who has authority.
Sometimes it uses silence like punishment.
Sometimes it quotes Scripture while refusing to imitate Christ.
And perhaps nobody outside the house knows.
But the children do.
They may not possess the vocabulary for contempt.
They just know something changes in Mom's face when Dad talks that way.
Father, this is not written to crush you.
It is written because there is still time to change what your children are watching.
The Gospel is not merely the announcement that guilty people can be forgiven someday when they die.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ saves sinners—and begins transforming them now.
Your failure does not need to become your family's permanent inheritance.
Repentance can interrupt what has been passed down for generations.
Maybe your father mocked your mother.
Maybe his father mocked his.
Maybe tenderness was considered weakness in the house where you grew up.
Maybe nobody ever taught you how to disagree without becoming cruel.
Maybe affection embarrassed the men in your family.
Maybe apology was practically nonexistent.
Maybe you promised yourself:
“I will never become my father.”
Then one afternoon you heard his voice coming out of your own mouth.
That moment can terrify a man.
But it can also awaken him.
Because generational patterns are powerful...
but Jesus Christ is more powerful than what was modeled for you.
You are not required to hand your children every wound your father handed you.
You can repent.
You can learn.
You can kneel.
You can apologize.
You can become teachable.
You can ask Christ to expose the pride you have learned to call personality.
And you can let your children witness something perhaps even more powerful than an apparently flawless father:
a repentant one.
Paul returns to the husband near the end of Ephesians 5 and writes:
“...let each one of you love his wife as himself...”
—Ephesians 5:33
Then the verse addresses the wife's reverence toward her husband as well.
Biblical marriage does not erase either spouse's responsibility before God.
But husband, when Scripture speaks directly to you, do not use the next person's command to escape your own.
You answer to Christ for yours.
Your wife's failures do not transform contempt into obedience.
Her imperfections do not cancel Ephesians 5:25.
The standard remains:
“As Christ loved the church.”
And this matters because Christ's love for His people was not earned by their perfection.
Scripture says:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
This does not mean a husband enables sin, tolerates abuse, avoids necessary boundaries, or pretends wrongdoing is acceptable.
Biblical love can confront.
Biblical love can establish wise boundaries.
Biblical love speaks truth.
But Christian truth is never permission for contempt.
The Christ who overturned tables is also the Christ who washed feet.
And the husband commanded to imitate Christ cannot selectively imitate only the parts of strength that make him feel powerful while ignoring the sacrificial love that calls his pride to die.
Maybe tonight your children will hear you speak to their mother.
What will they learn?
Will your son learn that masculinity needs humiliation to feel strong?
Or will he learn that strength can lower its voice?
Will your daughter learn that marriage means slowly disappearing underneath somebody else's contempt?
Or will she learn that covenant love carries dignity?
Will they learn that Christians say beautiful things publicly and become different people behind closed doors?
Or will they discover that Jesus changes the atmosphere of a home?
Think about something painfully simple.
One day your children may stand beside hospital beds.
One day they may become husbands and wives.
One day they may hold newborn babies and wonder what kind of homes they want to build.
And somewhere inside them will be thousands of tiny memories.
Dad opening the door for Mom.
Dad mocking Mom.
Dad thanking Mom.
Dad interrupting Mom.
Dad defending Mom.
Dad embarrassing Mom.
Dad praying with Mom.
Dad apologizing to Mom.
Dad speaking tenderly about Mom when she could not hear him.
Dad saying something cruel and never taking responsibility.
You are creating memories while thinking you are merely having conversations.
That is fatherhood under observation.
And no father gets this perfectly right.
That is exactly why fathers need Jesus.
Not merely Jesus as an inspirational example.
Jesus as Savior.
Jesus as Lord.
Jesus as the One who forgives actual sin.
Jesus as the One who exposes hidden pride.
Jesus as the One who transforms hearts that self-help cannot resurrect.
Perhaps you have already failed here.
Badly.
Maybe your children are older.
Maybe they remember.
Maybe your marriage has scars.
Maybe some words cannot be taken back.
You cannot crawl into yesterday and unsay them.
But you can decide what your children hear next.
Perhaps they need to hear:

“Kids, the way I have sometimes spoken to your mother was wrong. It was not Christlike. Do not imitate that part of me. I have asked God to forgive me, and I have asked your mother to forgive me. I want Jesus to change me.”
Do you know how much courage that requires?
Your children may remember your failure.
But now they will also remember your repentance.
And repentance is one of the greatest lessons a father can model.
Because your children do not need a father who convinces them he has never sinned.
They need a father who shows them where sinners go.
To Jesus.
This is the scandal of grace.
The guilty are invited home.
The proud can kneel.
The cruel can repent.
The wounded can learn tenderness.
The emotionally distant can learn presence.
The man who inherited dysfunction does not have to make dysfunction his children's inheritance.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the ugly chapters never happened.
Grace does something more astonishing.
Christ enters the chapter we wish we could erase...
and begins writing redemption from there.
So husband, honor your wife when the children are watching.
Honor her when they are not.
Speak about her with dignity.
Thank her where your children can hear it.
Let them watch you serve without demanding applause.
Let them hear you apologize without adding, “but you...”
Let them see affection that does not embarrass itself.
Let them discover that Christian masculinity is not threatened by tenderness.
And when you fail—and you will—run quickly toward repentance instead of self-defense.
Your children are watching what you do with your sin too.
Maybe this article exposed something you have been minimizing.
Do not hide from that conviction.
Take it to Christ.
Let other believers know they are not the only imperfect people desperately needing a perfect Savior.
Not because every sentence is comfortable, but because there may come a day when anger rises and you need to remember that little ears are listening.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and supporting a Christian ministry does not make anyone more righteous before God. We are saved by grace through faith in Christ, not by works.

But if this truth glorifies Christ and you believe another husband, father, son, brother, struggling believer, or even an unbelieving friend needs to encounter it, sharing becomes a simple way of putting truth where someone else may find it.
Send this privately to the man who may receive it better from a friend than from his wounded wife.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who knows something has gone cold.
Invite the seeker who is beginning to wonder whether Jesus really can change a human life.
Invite the man who never learned how to love because nobody ever showed him.
Because maybe the next generation does not need another father who knows how to win every argument.
Maybe they need to watch a father lose his pride at the feet of Jesus.
And perhaps years from now, when your children describe what love looked like in their childhood home, they will not remember a perfect father.
They will remember something better.
A man Christ kept changing.
A man who learned to repent.
A man who learned to honor their mother.
A man whose voice became gentler because Jesus became greater.
And when your children someday speak to the people they love, perhaps you will hear an echo of the grace they first heard from you.
Because little ears eventually become adult voices—and what they heard as children may become the language of the homes they build.
